title: “But he lied unto him” — why did the old prophet of Bethel lie to the man of God?
summary: An old prophet of Bethel tells the man of God from Judah that an angel has ordered him to bring him home to eat, and the narrator adds “But he lied unto him.” The man of God eats, is sentenced by the word of the Lord spoken through the same old prophet, and is killed by a lion. The verses read state the lie and its result; they do not state why the old prophet told it.
text: KJV 1 Kings 13:9: “For so was it charged me by the word of the Lord, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest.” KJV 13:11: “Now there dwelt an old prophet in Bethel; and his sons came and told him all the works that the man of God had done that day in Bethel” KJV 13:15: “Then he said unto him, Come home with me, and eat bread.” KJV 13:18: “He said unto him, I am a prophet also as thou art; and an angel spake unto me by the word of the Lord, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house, that he may eat bread and drink water. But he lied unto him.” KJV 13:19: “So he went back with him, and did eat bread in his house, and drank water.” KJV 13:20: “And it came to pass, as they sat at the table, that the word of the Lord came unto the prophet that brought him back:” KJV 13:21: “Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the Lord” KJV 13:22: “thy carcase shall not come unto the sepulchre of thy fathers.” KJV 13:24: “And when he was gone, a lion met him by the way, and slew him” KJV 13:26: “It is the man of God, who was disobedient unto the word of the Lord” KJV 13:30: “And he laid his carcase in his own grave; and they mourned over him, saying, Alas, my brother!” KJV 13:31: “When I am dead, then bury me in the sepulchre wherein the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones” KJV 13:32: “For the saying which he cried by the word of the Lord against the altar in Bethel” … “shall surely come to pass.” KJV 2 Kings 23:18: “And he said, Let him alone; let no man move his bones. So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet that came out of Samaria.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 13:18: וּמַלְאָ֡ךְ דִּבֶּ֣ר אֵלַי֩ בִּדְבַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה [and an angel spoke to me by the word of the Lord] … כִּחֵ֖שׁ לֹֽו [he lied to him]. 13:31: אֵ֚צֶל עַצְמֹתָ֔יו הַנִּ֖יחוּ אֶת־עַצְמֹתָֽי [beside his bones lay my bones]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 13:18: καὶ ἐψεύσατο αὐτῷ [and he lied to him]. 13:31: παρὰ τὰ ὀστᾶ αὐτοῦ θέτε με, ἵνα σωθῶσι τὰ ὀστᾶ μου μετὰ τῶν ὀστῶν αὐτοῦ [lay me beside his bones, that my bones may be preserved with his bones]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/13/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI13.htm.
reasoning: The chapter states a good deal about the old prophet. His sons told him what the man of God had done and said (13:11); he rode after him and invited him home (13:15); when refused, he claimed an angel’s command, and the narrator says in the same verse that this was a lie (13:18). The word of the Lord then came to that same prophet at the table, and he spoke the sentence (13:20–22). After the death he said the man “was disobedient unto the word of the Lord” (13:26), buried him in his own grave, mourned “Alas, my brother!”, asked to be buried beside him, and affirmed that the saying against the altar “shall surely come to pass” (13:30–32). What none of these verses gives is the reason for the lie. The gap matters to the passage: the man of God had been charged to eat no bread there (13:9), he had refused the same invitation once (13:16–17), the lie is the stated means by which he was brought back, and his death follows from it.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the old prophet wished to test whether the man of God would keep his charge; that he wanted the company or the honour of a man whose word had just been confirmed by a sign; that he acted for Bethel and its altar, to undo or discredit the message; that he sought a tie with the man of God for his own sake, in the light of his later request to lie in the same grave. Limits: the narrator’s words fix that the claim of an angel was a lie and do not describe the speaker’s purpose; the chapter records no reproof of the old prophet in the verses read, and that is not evidence of how the act was judged; the sentence at 13:21–22 is addressed to the man of God and names his own disobedience as its ground. The Greek of 13:31 has the added words “that my bones may be preserved with his bones”: that states a purpose for the burial request, not for the lie, and 2 Kings 23:18 reports that both sets of bones were left alone. It is a wording difference stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. Check made: 1 Kings 13:1–34 was read in the KJV, verses 11, 14–23, 26 and 29–32 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; 2 Kings 23:17–18 was read in the KJV; a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “lied” finds 1 Kings 13:18, Psalms 78:36, Isaiah 57:11 and Acts 5:4, and a search for “old prophet” finds 1 Kings 13:11, 13:25 and 13:29 and Luke 9:8 and 9:19. Those are word searches and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of the whole Bible; a passage that speaks of this man in other words would not be found by them. These checked verses do not say why the old prophet lied. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Elijah is told to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha — did Elijah anoint any of them?
summary: At Horeb the Lord tells Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu king over Israel and Elisha prophet in his place. In the verses read, Elijah casts his mantle on Elisha; it is Elisha who tells Hazael he will be king; and a young prophet sent by Elisha pours oil on Jehu. The verses read report no anointing done by Elijah, and they do not say how the command given to him was carried out.
text: KJV 1 Kings 19:15: “And the Lord said unto him, Go, return on thy way to the wilderness of Damascus: and when thou comest, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria:” KJV 19:16: “And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.” KJV 19:19: “and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.” KJV 19:21: “Then he arose, and went after Elijah, and ministered unto him.” KJV 2 Kings 2:13: “He took up also the mantle of Elijah that fell from him” KJV 2 Kings 8:13: “And Elisha answered, The Lord hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria.” KJV 2 Kings 8:15: “and Hazael reigned in his stead.” KJV 2 Kings 9:1: “And Elisha the prophet called one of the children of the prophets, and said unto him, Gird up thy loins, and take this box of oil in thine hand, and go to Ramothgilead” KJV 2 Kings 9:3: “Then take the box of oil, and pour it on his head, and say, Thus saith the Lord, I have anointed thee king over Israel.” KJV 2 Kings 9:6: “and he poured the oil on his head, and said unto him, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, I have anointed thee king over the people of the Lord, even over Israel.” KJV 2 Chronicles 22:7: “Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom the Lord had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 19:15: וּבָ֗אתָ וּמָשַׁחְתָּ֧ אֶת־חֲזָאֵ֛ל לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־אֲרָֽם [and you shall come and anoint Hazael as king over Aram]. 19:16: תִּמְשַׁ֥ח לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל [you shall anoint as king over Israel] … תִּמְשַׁ֥ח לְנָבִ֖יא תַּחְתֶּֽיךָ [you shall anoint as prophet in your place]. 19:19: וַיַּשְׁלֵ֥ךְ אַדַּרְתֹּ֖ו אֵלָֽיו [and he cast his mantle to him]. 2 Kings 9:6: וַיִּצֹ֥ק הַשֶּׁ֖מֶן אֶל־רֹאשֹׁ֑ו [and he poured the oil on his head]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 19:15: καὶ ἥξεις καὶ χρίσεις τὸν Ἀζαὴλ εἰς βασιλέα τῆς Συρίας [and you shall come and anoint Azael to be king of Syria]. 19:16: χρίσεις εἰς προφήτην ἀντὶ σοῦ [you shall anoint to be prophet in your place]. 19:19: καὶ ἐπέῥῥιψε τὴν μηλωτὴν αὐτοῦ ἐπʼ αὐτόν [and he cast his mantle upon him]. 2 Kings 8:13: ἔδειξέ μοι Κύριός σε βασιλεύοντα ἐπὶ Συρίαν [the Lord has shown me you reigning over Syria]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/19/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/9/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI19.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2KI08.htm.
reasoning: The command is in the second person and names three acts for Elijah: “anoint Hazael”, Jehu “shalt thou anoint”, Elisha “shalt thou anoint”. The verses read report something for each of the three men. Elijah finds Elisha and casts his mantle on him, and Elisha follows and serves him (19:19–21); the verse names a mantle and does not name oil or use the word “anoint”. With Hazael it is Elisha who speaks, at Damascus, and his words are that the Lord has shown him that Hazael will be king (2 Kings 8:13); no oil and no word “anoint” stands in 8:7–15. Jehu is anointed with oil, by “one of the children of the prophets” whom Elisha sends (2 Kings 9:1–6). The order also differs: the command names Hazael, Jehu, Elisha, and the account tells of Elisha, Hazael, Jehu. The gap matters because the command is the Lord’s answer to Elijah at Horeb and sets out what is to follow; the verses read do not say whether Elijah did any of the three acts himself, or by what step the task passed to Elisha.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that Elijah carried out the command through his successor, so that what Elisha did or ordered counts as done by Elijah; that “anoint” is used here for appointing or designating, so that the mantle and the spoken word answer to it; that Elijah did anoint one or more of the three in acts the books do not report; that the command was left in part undone by Elijah. Limits: the command sets no time and does not say that Elijah must act in person at each step; that an act is not reported does not show that it was not done; 2 Chronicles 22:7 says the Lord had anointed Jehu and names no human hand; the casting of the mantle is not called an anointing in the verses read, and it is not said there to be anything else. Check made: 1 Kings 19:15–17 and 19:19–21 and 2 Kings 2:13, 8:7–15 and 9:1–10 were read in the KJV, and 1 Kings 19:15–17 and 19:19–21, 2 Kings 8:13 and 9:1–3 and 9:6 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; a search of the packaged KJV for verses that have “anoint”, “anointed” or “anointing” together with “Hazael”, “Jehu” or “Elisha” finds 1 Kings 19:15, 1 Kings 19:16 and 2 Chronicles 22:7; a search of 1 Kings for those three words finds 1:34, 1:39, 1:45, 5:1, 19:15 and 19:16, and of 2 Kings finds 9:3, 9:6, 9:12, 11:12 and 23:30. Those are word searches and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of 1 and 2 Kings in full; an account that uses other words would not be found by them. These checked verses do not report an anointing by Elijah of Hazael, of Jehu or of Elisha. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Twelve pieces, ten tribes and “one tribe” — which tribe is the twelfth?
summary: Ahijah tears a garment into twelve pieces, gives Jeroboam ten for “ten tribes”, and says Solomon’s son shall have “one tribe”. Ten and one make eleven. In the KJV and the Hebrew, the verses read do not say whose the twelfth piece is or which tribe it stands for; Brenton’s Greek reads “two tribes” at 11:32 and 11:36.
text: KJV 1 Kings 11:13: “Howbeit I will not rend away all the kingdom; but will give one tribe to thy son” KJV 11:30: “And Ahijah caught the new garment that was on him, and rent it in twelve pieces:” KJV 11:31: “And he said to Jeroboam, Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee:” KJV 11:32: “But he shall have one tribe for my servant” KJV 11:35: “But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand, and will give it unto thee, even ten tribes.” KJV 11:36: “And unto his son will I give one tribe” KJV 12:20: “there was none that followed the house of David, but the tribe of Judah only.” KJV 12:21: “he assembled all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin” KJV 12:23: “unto all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the remnant of the people” KJV 2 Chronicles 11:12: “having Judah and Benjamin on his side.” KJV Joshua 19:1: “and their inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 11:30: שְׁנֵ֥ים עָשָׂ֖ר קְרָעִֽים [twelve pieces]. 11:31: וְנָתַתִּ֣י לְךָ֔ אֵ֖ת עֲשָׂרָ֥ה הַשְּׁבָטִֽים [and I will give you the ten tribes]. 11:32: וְהַשֵּׁ֥בֶט הָאֶחָ֖ד יִֽהְיֶה־לֹּ֑ו [and the one tribe shall be his]. 11:36: וְלִבְנֹ֖ו אֶתֵּ֣ן שֵֽׁבֶט־אֶחָ֑ד [and to his son I will give one tribe]. 12:20: זוּלָתִ֥י שֵֽׁבֶט־יְהוּדָ֖ה לְבַדֹּֽו [except the tribe of Judah alone]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 11:13: σκῆπτρον ἓν δώσω τῷ υἱῷ σου [one tribe I will give to your son]. 11:30: δώδεκα ῥήγματα [twelve pieces]. 11:31: καὶ δώσω σοι δέκα σκῆπτρα [and I will give you ten tribes]. 11:32: Καὶ δύο σκῆπτρα ἔσονται αὐτῷ [and two tribes shall be his]. 11:36: Τῷ δὲ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ δώσω τὰ δύο σκῆπτρα [and to his son I will give the two tribes]. 12:20: πάρεξ σκήπτρου Ἰούδα καὶ Βενιαμὶν μόνοι [except the tribe of Judah and Benjamin alone]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/11/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/12/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI11.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI12.htm.
reasoning: The sign gives the numbers itself: twelve pieces (11:30), ten to Jeroboam for “ten tribes” (11:31, 11:35), and “one tribe” for Solomon’s line (11:13, 11:32, 11:36). The prophet does not say what becomes of the two remaining pieces, and the sum of the tribes named is eleven. The account that follows says first that none followed the house of David “but the tribe of Judah only” (12:20) and in the next verse that Rehoboam gathered “all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin” (12:21). So in the KJV and the Hebrew quoted, the verses read leave open which tribe the twelfth piece stands for and on which side it is counted. The gap matters because the sign is the stated ground of the division of the kingdom, and the count is its content. The Greek quoted does give a count that reaches twelve at two of the verses: it has “two tribes” at 11:32 and 11:36 and “Judah and Benjamin” at 12:20, while at 11:13 it has “one tribe”, as the Hebrew does.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the KJV and Hebrew verses quoted state: that the twelfth tribe is Benjamin, held with Judah by Rehoboam (12:21, 12:23; 2 Chronicles 11:12), and that “one tribe” means one beside Judah, David’s own; that “one tribe” is Judah, with Benjamin or Simeon counted within it (Joshua 19:1 places Simeon’s inheritance inside Judah’s); that Levi, which had no territory of its own, is the tribe left out of the count; that “ten” and “one” are round figures for the greater part and the lesser. The Greek quoted states the count of two at 11:32 and 11:36; it does not name the two there, and it names Judah and Benjamin at 12:20. Limits: the sign does not say that every piece stands for one tribe on one side, though 11:31 ties ten pieces to ten tribes; a list of the twelve tribes is not given in these verses, and the Bible counts the tribes in more than one way, so which names make up the “ten” is not fixed by the verses read; 12:20 and 12:21 can both be true if Benjamin joined Rehoboam after the people made Jeroboam king, a step the text does not report; the Greek readings are wording differences stated here and not proposed as a separate finding. Check made: 1 Kings 11:29–43 and 12:15, 12:17, 12:20, 12:21 and 12:23 were read in the KJV, and 11:13, 11:30–32, 11:35–36 and 12:20–21 and 12:23 also in the Hebrew and the Greek; a search of the packaged KJV for “ten tribes” finds 1 Kings 11:31 and 11:35 only, for “twelve pieces” Judges 19:29 and 1 Kings 11:30, and for the whole words “one tribe” Numbers 36:9, Judges 21:3 and 21:6 and 1 Kings 11:13, 11:32 and 11:36. Those are word searches and a reading of the verses listed, not a reading of Kings and Chronicles in full. These checked verses, in the KJV and the Hebrew, do not say which tribe is the twelfth. title: “The book of the acts of Solomon” — what was this book, and is it the source Chronicles names?
summary: For the rest of Solomon’s acts and his wisdom, 1 Kings sends the reader to “the book of the acts of Solomon”. A phrase search of the packaged KJV finds that title in this verse only. At the same point 2 Chronicles names three other writings. The verses read do not say who wrote the book, what it held beyond the words quoted, or whether it is the same as any of the three.
text: KJV 1 Kings 11:41: “And the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the book of the acts of Solomon?” KJV 1 Kings 14:19: “behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.” KJV 1 Kings 14:29: “are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?” KJV 2 Chronicles 9:29: “Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are they not written in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nebat?” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Kings 11:41: הֲלֹֽוא־הֵ֣ם כְּתֻבִ֔ים עַל־סֵ֖פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י שְׁלֹמֹֽה [are they not written on the book of the words (or acts) of Solomon?]. 2 Chronicles 9:29: הֲלֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ נָתָ֣ן הַנָּבִ֔יא [are they not written on the words of Nathan the prophet]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1 Kings 11:41: οὐκ ἰδοὺ ταῦτα γέγραπται ἐν βιβλίῳ ῥημάτων Σαλωμών; [behold, are not these written in a book of the words of Solomon?]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/11/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/14/9/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1KI11.htm.
reasoning: The verse names the book by a title and says what is in it: “the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom”. That much is stated. The verses read do not say who wrote it, when, or where it was kept, and the account of Solomon closes by pointing to it for what the account itself leaves out. From the next reign onward the same formula points to differently named books, “the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel” (14:19) and “of the kings of Judah” (14:29). At the matching place 2 Chronicles 9:29 points instead to “the book of Nathan the prophet”, “the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite” and “the visions of Iddo the seer”. The gap matters because the verse rests the completeness of its account of Solomon on a writing that the reader is expected to be able to consult.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that the book was a record of Solomon’s reign kept at court, distinct from the later “chronicles of the kings”; that it is the same body of writing that 2 Chronicles 9:29 cites under the names of Nathan, Ahijah and Iddo; that it was a collection that held sayings as well as deeds, in view of “and his wisdom”; that it has not survived. Limits: the two books may point to different writings for the same reign without conflict, and no conflict is asserted here; that a title is found in one verse by a phrase search does not show that the writing is not meant elsewhere under another name; whether any existing writing is this book is not something these verses settle; the Hebrew word in the title can mean “words” or “acts”, and the KJV has “acts” for it in both halves of the verse. Check made: 1 Kings 11:41–43, 14:19 and 14:29 and 2 Chronicles 9:29 were read in the KJV, and 1 Kings 11:41 and 2 Chronicles 9:29 also in the Hebrew and 1 Kings 11:41 in the Greek; a phrase search of the packaged KJV for “acts of Solomon” finds 1 Kings 11:41 and 2 Chronicles 9:29, and for “book of the acts” finds 1 Kings 11:41 only. Those are phrase searches, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not say who wrote the book of the acts of Solomon or whether it is one of the writings named at 2 Chronicles 9:29.
